docs.title: Adding Custom Analyses
Adding Custom Analyses¶
docs.text: Learn how to create and integrate custom analyses into the Model Live Diagnostics (MLD) package. By the end of this tutorial, you will know how to implement a custom analysis that automatically generates interactive UI controls based on user selection. Any analysis that can be computed with xarray and plotted via matplotlib.pyplot can be integrated into the analysis section.

docs.title: Prerequisites¶
docs.text:
Before starting, ensure you have:

  • Started an MLD session in your current notebook or kernel (your custom recipes must be written in this same environment)
  • Loaded a catalogue and dataset.

For setup guidance, refer to the Getting Started Tutorial.

docs.title: Analysis Interface¶
docs.text: The Analysis section provides a dropdown menu of predefined analyses (and user-defined analyses once they are added!). Selecting an analysis dynamically populates the interface with the required input widgets.

docs.title: How a recipe runs¶
docs.text:
When you click Plot data in the analysis section, MLD does this:

recipe(ds, **options_from_widgets)
        │
        ├── returns DataArray                 ──► plotted with MLD's defaults
        └── returns (DataArray, plot_kwargs)  ──► plotted with your settings
  • ds: the first argument is the dataset currently loaded in the UI. MLD passes this automatically, so no widget is generated for it.
  • Keyword Arguments: Every subsequent argument generates a UI widget based on its type annotation. The user's input is passed to your recipe as that keyword argument.
  • Return Value: The UI automatically handles plotting. To customise the plot's appearance, your recipe must return a tuple containing the DataArray and a plot_kwargs dictionary. This dictionary exclusively controls the plot styling.

docs.title: Building a custom analysis¶
docs.text: The MLD package is designed to require minimal modifications to a typical analysis written for an xarray.DataArray.

docs.title: The Minimum Recipe¶
docs.text:
If your analysis hardcodes specific variables or dimensions and you are happy with the default plotting style, your recipe can be a simple, standard Python function.

Important: To be compatible with MLD, the function must accept an xr.Dataset as its first argument and return an xr.DataArray. These are the strict minimum requirements for any analysis.

docs.title: Building a Recipe That Takes Arguments¶
docs.text:
Let's build on the minimum recipe. What if we want to generalise it so we can easily select any variable or dimension to average?

To do this, we define the function arguments using typing.Annotated. MLD reads these annotations to automatically understand what type of data the function expects.

docs.title: Defining arguments¶
docs.text:
Each argument after ds must be declared like this:

name: Annotated[<python type>, {<metadata>}] = <default>
View metadata keys configuration Key Required? Effect "kind" Recommended Chooses the widget (see the table below). If you leave it out, you get a plain text box and your recipe receives a string. "name" Recommended The label shown on the widget (e.g., "Select Depth Slice"). If you leave it out, the label defaults to the argument name (e.g., lvl_dim). "description" Recommended Shown as the widget's tooltip. (Note: Checkboxes cannot display tooltips). "units" Optional Appended to the widget label (e.g., Select Depth Slice (m)). "choices" Only for "kind": "choice" The list of options for the dropdown menu.

UI Labels vs. Code Variables

"name" only changes what is displayed in the UI. The value is always passed to your recipe under the argument name, so var: Annotated[float, {"name":"Variable", ...}] still arrives as var=...

View supported "kind" values and widgets "kind" Widget Options come from Your recipe receives "data variable" Dropdown ds.data_vars (the variables in the loaded dataset) str "dimension" Dropdown The dataset's coordinates and dimensions str (or None) "choice" Dropdown Your "choices" list Whatever the chosen item is "float" Number box — float "int" Whole-number box — int "bool" Checkbox — bool "str" Text box — str

docs.title: Using plot_kwargs¶
docs.text:
You can ensure the plot is created exactly how you want by adding a plot_kwargs dictionary to your return statement. To use this feature, your function must return a two-item tuple: (DataArray, plot_kwargs).

When MLD receives this dictionary, it looks for four specific keys to configure the figure and axes. Any other keys you include are passed directly to the underlying xarray.plot() method.

Key Expected Type Effect "figsize" tuple Sets the dimensions of the figure (defaults to (6, 4)). "title" str Sets the plot title (defaults to the DataArray name). "ax_kwargs" dict Passed to ax.set() to modify axis properties (e.g., xlabel, ylim, yscale). "customise" callable or list A function (or list of functions) that accepts (ax, data). These run last, allowing you to add complex matplotlib features.

Here is an example of a recipe returning custom plot settings:

docs.title: Advanced plot customisation¶
docs.text:
While plot_kwargs handles standard xarray plotting arguments, you may want to add features like shaded bands, reference lines, annotations, a second axis, or a custom legend. You can achieve this by passing custom Matplotlib functions to the "customise" key in your plot_kwargs dictionary.

Any function you pass to "customise" must accept exactly two positional arguments:

  1. ax: The matplotlib.axes.Axes object MLD generated for the plot (note: ax.figure accesses the whole Figure).
  2. data: The exact xarray.DataArray returned by your recipe.

They run in list order, after ax_kwargs, so they can override anything.

Compute your data once

The loaded dataset is lazy (backed by Dask), so your recipe's result is only calculated when it is used. If your customise functions also read data (e.g., to fit a trend line), call .compute() on the result before returning it. The calculation then runs once, rather than once for the plot and again for every customise function.

The following example defines a custom function that draws a bounding box with an annotated arrow, and appends it to the base heatmap:

docs.title: Ready-made customisations¶
docs.text: MLD provides several built-in customisation functions for common meteorological and oceanographic visualisations in the med_diagnostics.plot_customisations module. These will be updated as the package is developed, and full details can be found in the API Reference.

docs.title: Passing extra arguments to a customise function¶
docs.text:
Because MLD strictly calls your function with exactly two arguments—func(ax, data)—you cannot pass additional keyword arguments directly through the MLD pipeline.

If your custom function requires external settings (like a specific threshold value or a colour string), you must fix those arguments in advance using a lambda function:

docs.title: Full control: Secondary axes and custom plot types¶
docs.text:
Because the ax object you receive represents the entire plot, a customise function can do absolutely anything Matplotlib is capable of doing.

Adding secondary axes or moving legends: You can easily inject secondary axes (e.g., converting Celsius to Fahrenheit) or restructure the plot layout:

def twin_axis_in_fahrenheit(ax, data):
    """Add a right-hand axis in °F."""
    ax.secondary_yaxis(
        "right", functions=(lambda c: c * 9 / 5 + 32, lambda f: (f - 32) * 5 / 9)
    ).set_ylabel("°F")

def legend_outside(ax, data):
    """Move the legend outside the axes."""
    ax.legend(loc="upper left", bbox_to_anchor=(1.01, 1))
    ax.figure.tight_layout()

Replacing the default plot entirely: By default, MLD always draws data.plot(...) first. If you want a plot type that xarray does not natively produce (such as a custom bar chart or specialized scatter plot), your customise function can clear the axes and draw its own.

Important: Calling ax.clear() also removes the title and ax_kwargs that MLD already applied, so you must explicitly set them again inside your custom function:

def bar_chart(ax, data):
    """Replace the default xarray plot with a Matplotlib bar chart."""
    
    # 1. Erase the default xarray plot MLD just drew
    ax.clear()
    
    # 2. Draw your custom plot
    ax.bar(data["time"].dt.year, data.values, color="tab:blue")
    
    # 3. Re-apply essential formatting that was cleared
    ax.set(title=data.name, xlabel="Year")

docs.title: Checklist¶
docs.text:
Use the checklist below to help upload a new recipe to MLD:

  • The first argument is the dataset (ds: xr.Dataset).
  • Every other argument is Annotated[type, {"kind": ...}] with one of "data variable", "dimension", "choice", "float", "int", "bool", or "str".
  • Every other argument has a default value.
  • "choice" arguments include a "choices" list in the metadata dictionary (or use a Literal[...] type).
  • Optional dimensions are typed str | None with a default of None.
  • The docstring's first line states what the recipe computes, and its second paragraph details which grid or models it targets.
  • The function returns either a DataArray, or a tuple of (DataArray, plot_kwargs).
  • You have clicked Refresh analysis recipes in the UI after uploading or updating your function.

docs.title: Contributing a recipe¶
docs.text:
Because custom recipes integrate seamlessly into the MLD pipeline, they are perfectly structured to be included as inbuilt recipes. If you have created an analysis that would be useful to others, you can submit it to the core repository, making it available for others to use.

For full details on how to format, test, and submit your code via a pull request, please see the Contributing Recipes guide.

docs.title: Advanced Usage
docs.text: To get started with model live diagnostics, please see the getting started tutorial. The following guide provides further information about the options available within the package.

docs.title: 1. Create live model session¶
docs.text:
• model_type: str (Type of ACCESS model, use one of the following):
    • CM2
    • CM3
    • OM2
    • OM3
    • EM15
    • EM16
    • MOM6
  • model_path: str (Path to model output directory/files on Gadi.)

The CreateModelDiagnosticsSession() class instance triggers the following tasks in the background:

  • Start the dask cluster
  • Retrieve the most up-to-date nominated model data and build a new ESM datastore, using the ACCESS-NRI intake catalog. N.B. This is saved as a compressed *.csv in the user's $HOME directory on Gadi. If a catalog already exitsts within the user's $HOME directory, and is valid and up to date, the datastore is not overwritten.
  • Initialises the HoloViz Panel widget, and creates the orange 'catalog', blue 'status', and red 'warning' information boxes.
import med_diagnostics

session = med_diagnostics.session.CreateModelDiagnosticsSession(
    model_type="OM2", model_path="path/to/your/live/model/data/output"
)

docs.title: 2. Access to Data¶
docs.text: While the UI provides a quick way to visualise your model runs, advanced users may wish to interact directly with the underlying data structures for custom analysis in their Jupyter Notebook.

docs.title: Retrieve the Data Catalogue¶
docs.text:
You can extract the active Intake-ESM datastore object directly from your session.

  • A convenience function to return the currently loaded live model data catalogue.
  • Returns: An Intake catalogue containing the user's model data.
  • Return type: intake-esm datastore object.
datastore = session.return_model_data_catalog()
datastore

docs.title: Retrieve a loaded Dataset¶
docs.text:
You can extract the loaded dataset object directly from your session.

  • A convenience function to return the currently loaded dataset.
  • Returns: An xarray dataset containing the user's model data.
  • Return type: ``xarray` dataset.
dataset = session.return_loaded_dataset()
dataset

docs.title: 3. Define a custom analysis to be performed in MLD¶
docs.text: Please see the x tutorial to see in detail how to add a custom analysis recipe.

docs.title: 4. Session Management¶
docs.text:
To free up compute resources on Gadi, it is best practice to close the Dask client when you have finished your analysis.

  • This safely closes the Dask client to end the current CreateModelDiagnosticsSession instance.
session.end_session()

docs.title: 5. Troubleshooting and UI Warnings¶
docs.text:
The interface features built-in error handling to prevent crashes from invalid visualisations or missing data. When an issue occurs or the interface automates a step, a red warning bar will appear at the top of the UI.

Common triggers for these warnings include:

  • Invalid Plot Configurations: Attempting to assign the same dimension to multiple axes, or selecting a complex plot type (like a Heatmap or Animation) for a dataset that lacks the required dimensions. In these cases, the UI will prompt you to fix the axes or automatically downgrade your selection to a Line plot.
  • Missing Overlay Data: When using the multiplot feature, you may load reference models that do not contain the matching dataset or the specific variable you are attempting to plot. The interface will warn you and automatically drop these incompatible models from the overlay.
  • Automated Plotting: If a dataset only has one viable dimension for a Line plot, the UI will briefly warn you that it is bypassing the axis selection step to generate the plot automatically.
  • Analysis Recipe Failures If a predefined recipe has an invalid configuration passed to it, or if there is an error in a user defined recipe, details will appear in the warning textbox in the analysis section.

If a plot fails to generate, review the red warning bar and adjust your dropdown selections accordingly. The warning message will clear automatically once a valid plot is successfully generated.

docs.title: Getting Started Tutorial
docs.text:
The Model Live Diagnostics framework is designed to provide useful and practical Jupyter-based tools for the monitoring and diagnostic analyses of currently running (aka ‘live’) ACCESS climate models on the Australian NCI supercomputer Gadi.

The ACCESS-NRI Model Live Diagnostics package, and the tools that support it, are still a work in progress. We value your feedback, especially in the form of reporting issues/bugs or suggesting ways to improve the framework. To do so, please open an issue here.

docs.title: What does this package do?¶
docs.text:
The primary purpose of the ACCESS-NRI Model Live Diagnostics package is to provide a simple, easy to use and accessible framework for the ACCESS modelling community to check, monitor, visualise and evaluate model behaviour and progress on currently running or ‘live’ ACCESS models on the Australian NCI supercomputer Gadi. In addition to monitoring a live model, the package provides the functionality to load, visualise and compare legacy ACCESS model data with the selected live user model.

This package is actively developed by the Model Evaluation Team at Australia's climate simulator (ACCESS-NRI). Version 2.0 introduces advanced visualisation capabilities to your live model analysis, including:

  • Interactive animations for visualising changes over time.
  • Multidimensional data slicing via dynamic interface sliders.
  • Calculated difference overlays (Reference vs. User data) for direct model comparisons.

The full docs for MLD can be found here.

docs.title: 0. Install and start an ARE Session¶
docs.text: As described in the homepage of this documentation, you need to clone the MLD repository and start an ARE JupyterLab Session.

docs.title: 1. Set up access¶
docs.text: Import the med_diagnostics package that has been cloned to an accessible project location on Gadi

docs.title: 2. Create live model session¶
docs.text:
• model_type: str (Type of ACCESS model (e.g. OM2 or CM2)).
  • model_path: str (Path to model output directory/files on Gadi.)

docs.title: Running CreateModelDiagnosticsSession() will start a session with interactive widgets for you to monitor your model run¶
docs.text:
i) Upon startup, the orange 'catalog', blue 'status', and red 'warning' information boxes will load. You will see the following session summary and blue status message while the new intake catalogue is being built from the live model data. Depending on the size of the model data, this can take a number of minutes. The Dask cluster address (in this case: /proxy/8787/status) can be used to monitor data retrieval by adding it to the 'Dask Dashboard URL' found in the left panel.

ii) Once the live model data catalogue has been successfully built, the blue status message will update and the orange status message will report the time and date of the last live model catalogue build.

iii) All available datasets from the selected model will be listed in the dropdown. Select the dataset you wish to monitor and click 'Load dataset'.

iv) Once loaded, the plotting interface will appear. From here, you can:

  • Select a variable: Choose a model variable from the dropdown list.
  • Choose a plot type: Select a Line plot, Heatmap, or Animation. Note that datasets with fewer dimensions may only support line plots.
  • Toggle variable names: Use the "Display variable long names" switch to toggle between long and short names if the defaults are unclear.

Once these options have been selected, press the green "Select Variable and Plot Type" button.

v) The UI options vary by plot type. To animate a heatmap over time, for instance, assign values to the X, Y, and Z axes as shown below: Once these options have been selected, press the green "Plot Data" button.

vi) If your dataset includes extra dimensions (e.g., ocean depth in OM2), sliders will appear so you can slice the data. Depending on the dataset and plot type, you may need to configure zero or more slices. Once you have selected your slice configuration, press the green "Confirm Slices & Plot" button, and your plot will begin to load.

docs.title: Optional:¶
docs.text: This process can be repeated with as many datasets, variables, and plot types as desired.

docs.title: 3.2. Loading and Plotting Reference Model Data (Optional)¶
docs.text:
The live model data can be compared with any alternative/legacy ACCESS models of the same type (e.g. CM2, OM2) found within the ACCESS-NRI Intake Catalogue.

i) The reference model dropdown menu is pre-filled with all available models of the same type from the ACCESS-NRI Intake Catalogue (in this example the list contains all models of type 'OM2'). Select the reference model of choice and click 'Load model'.

ii) Once the reference model loads, a new dropdown menu will appear displaying all of its available datasets. Select the dataset you wish to monitor and click 'Load dataset'.

iii) Once loaded, the standard UI for selecting a variable, plot type, axes, and slices will appear, allowing you to plot the desired data.

docs.title: Optional:¶
docs.text: This process can be repeated with as many datasets, variables, and plot types as desired.

docs.title: 3.3. Comparing User and Reference Models (Optional)¶
docs.text:
This section allows you to compare data by overlaying line plots or displaying heatmaps side-by-side. It also provides the option to plot the difference between the user and reference datasets to help highlight any discrepancies.

i) Select a reference model from the dropdown menu and click "Add reference model". If a dataset matching your loaded user dataset exists, it will load automatically; if no match is found, the model will be skipped. You can repeat this process to add as many reference models as you like. Finally, select your preferred plot type (Line plot or Heatmap (grid)) and click "Plot Loaded Datasets".

ii) Next, select your relevant axes and choose an analysis type from the dropdown menu. Your options are:

  • None (plot all loaded data): Plots the data overlaid (or side-by-side for heatmaps).
  • Plot Difference (Ref. - User data): Plots the calculated difference between the datasets.
  • Plot All Data & Difference: Displays both the loaded data and the calculated differences. Once configured, click the green "Plot Loaded Datasets" button, and if slices are required, the slice configuration UI will show.

iii) Once configured, click the 'Confirm Slices & Plot' button. The selected plots will then load.

docs.title: 4. End live model session¶
docs.text: The safest way to end the current live session is to use the session.end_session() function which ends both the dask and background scheduler processes.

docs.title: ACCESS-NRI Model Live Diagnostics
docs.text:
Welcome to the documentation and reference guide for the ACCESS-NRI Model Live Diagnostics package. Model Live Diagnostics provides practical Jupyter-based tools for interactive monitoring and diagnostic analysis of currently running, or "live", ACCESS climate models on the Australian NCI supercomputer Gadi.

The framework is intended for use in the Australian Research Environment (ARE) and is still under active development. Please report bugs and suggestions through the GitHub issue tracker.

docs.title: What does this package do?
docs.text:
Model Live Diagnostics helps the ACCESS modelling community check, monitor, visualise, and evaluate the behaviour and progress of live ACCESS models on Gadi. It can also load, visualise, and compare legacy ACCESS model data with the selected live user model.

Version 2.0 introduces:

  • Interactive animations for visualising changes over time.
  • Multidimensional data slicing via dynamic interface sliders.
  • Calculated difference overlays for direct reference-versus-user model comparisons.

docs.title: Quick-start guide
docs.text: The framework is intended for ARE JupyterLab sessions running on Gadi. Use outside Jupyter notebooks is not supported.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
Before starting, make sure you:

  1. Have an NCI account. See the NCI account documentation. You will also need to join a project with a compute allocation.
  2. Can access the projects containing your model data. The ACCESS-NRI Intake Catalog references data across multiple Gadi projects. See the supported project list and the NCI project access documentation.
  3. Are a member of the ACCESS-NRI xp65 project to access the ACCESS-NRI conda environment.

docs.title: Start an ARE JupyterLab session
docs.text:
1. Log in to ARE and start a JupyterLab instance. The recommended settings for these large datasets are:
Setting Recommendation Compute size XX-Large (28 CPUs, 126 GB memory) Storage For example, gdata/project1+gdata/project2

In Advanced options, use:

Setting Value Module directories /g/data/xp65/public/modules Modules conda/access-med
  1. Start the session with the ACCESS-NRI MED conda environment.
  2. Follow the Getting started tutorial to begin a Model Live Diagnostics session.

docs.title: Install the package directly
docs.text:
The package is pre-installed in the ACCESS-NRI MED conda environment. Alternatively, install it from the access-nri conda channel or PyPI:

condaPyPI 
conda install -c accessnri med-diagnostics

pip install med-diagnostics

Contributions to Model Live Diagnostics are always welcome. They can include code, documentation improvements, examples, bug reports, and feature suggestions.

docs.title: Contributing code
docs.text: Contributions to the code are welcome. If you would like to contribute, start by opening an issue describing what you would like to change and why. Repository maintainers may discuss the issue with you before inviting you to submit a pull request.

docs.title: Submitting pull requests
docs.text:
1. Fork this repository.
  2. Clone your fork locally, connect it to the upstream repository, and create a branch for your work. Include the issue number in the branch name when appropriate:
git clone git@github.com:YOUR_GITHUB_USERNAME/MED-live-diagnostics.git
cd MED-live-diagnostics
git remote add upstream git@github.com:ACCESS-NRI/MED-live-diagnostics.git
git checkout -b <issue#_description> main

This example assumes that you have SSH keys configured for GitHub. If you do not, replace git@github.com: with https://github.com/. 3. Make your code changes and test them. 4. Commit your edits, including docstrings, documentation updates, and unit tests. Please follow numpydoc style for docstrings where possible. 5. Open a pull request against the main branch of the MED-live-diagnostics repository.

docs.title: Contributing documentation
docs.text:
Adding documentation is always helpful. This may include:

  • Extending or clarifying existing documentation.
  • Adding examples of Model Live Diagnostics being used for live monitoring or analysis.
  • Improving docstrings, including adding examples.

The documentation is written in Markdown and built with MkDocs Material. Contributions should be submitted via pull requests to the MED-live-diagnostics repository.

docs.title: Preview the documentation locally
docs.text:
Install the documentation dependencies and start the local development server:

cd documentation
pip install -r requirements.txt
mkdocs serve

Build the static site with:

cd documentation
mkdocs build --strict

docs.title: Feature requests and bug reports
docs.text:
We welcome bug reports, feature requests, and other suggestions. Please submit them through the GitHub issue tracker.

When suggesting a feature, explain how it should work and keep the scope as narrow as possible. This makes features easier to implement.

When reporting a bug, include:

  • Details about your local setup, especially the Python interpreter version.
  • Detailed steps to reproduce the issue, ideally with a Minimal, Complete and Verifiable Example.
  • A demonstration test that currently fails but should pass when the issue is fixed, when possible.
